Case Vignette: "Margaret"

Margaret is a 67-year-old woman of Oceania descent, a widow, and a database administrator for a regional health network. She presents with a guarded posture, her hands folded tightly in her lap, her eyes frequently darting to the door of my office. She speaks in a low, measured voice, as if she is constantly listening for something else.

The story begins not with a single event, but with a slow, insidious erosion. Margaret met her husband, a charismatic and respected community leader, when she was 24. For the first two years, he was attentive and kind. The first time he struck her, it was a "mistake"-a slap during an argument about her working late. He wept, apologized, and promised it would never happen again. She believed him. That was the pattern for the next 35 years.

The abuse was cyclical. Periods of calm, almost suffocating tenderness, would be broken by a sudden escalation. A perceived slight-a dinner not to his liking, a phone call from a male colleague-could trigger a torrent of verbal abuse, then a shove, then a fist. Margaret learned to read the subtle shifts in his posture, the tightening of his jaw, the way his voice dropped an octave. She became an expert at placation, at making herself small, at erasing her own needs. She stopped seeing friends. She stopped wearing earrings he hadn't bought her. She told herself she was keeping the peace.

Her work as a database administrator became her sanctuary. In the clean, logical world of SQL queries and data schemas, there was no unpredictability. She could build structures that functioned perfectly, that made sense. She would stay late at the office, running reports that no one asked for, just to delay going home. Her colleagues saw her as quiet, efficient, and reliable-a "rock." They didn't know she was hiding bruises under long sleeves.

He died five years ago, of a sudden heart attack. Margaret felt a wave of relief so profound it terrified her. She told no one. The first year of widowhood was a strange, hollow peace. She cleaned out his closet, donated his suits, repainted the house. She thought she was healing.

But she wasn't. Now, at 67, Margaret cannot sleep without the bedroom door locked and a chair wedged under the handle. She checks the locks on her apartment three times before bed. She has not had a romantic relationship since his death. The thought of a man touching her-even a friendly hand on her shoulder-makes her skin crawl. She avoids crowded spaces, especially at night, because she feels a man's presence as a potential threat. At work, she has become hypervigilant. If a male colleague stands too close to her cubicle, her heart races, her palms sweat, and she feels a crushing pressure in her chest. She has begun to take her lunch break in her car, in the far corner of the parking lot, where she can see all the approaches.

She replays the arguments in her head, dissecting her own words, wondering what she could have done differently to avoid the blow. She has nightmares: she is drowning, or he is standing over her bed, his face a shadow. She wakes up gasping, her body rigid, drenched in sweat.

Last month, during a routine database migration, a junior developer made a joke about a "hostile takeover" of the server. Margaret froze. She could not speak. She excused herself and spent twenty minutes in the bathroom, trembling. She has not been able to sit in the same room as that developer since.

She came to see me because her primary care doctor found her blood pressure dangerously high and asked about her stress. Margaret told her, for the first time in her life, "I think I'm still scared." She is a woman who built a career on order and predictability, but the chaos of her past has become the only constant in her present. She is not sure how to live without the fear.
